source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / Directorate General of Agriculture, "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកសៀង" [Soybean cultivation techniques], official extension manual, 2018
text:
This 2018 official MAFF Directorate General of Agriculture extension manual, "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកសៀង" (Soybean cultivation techniques), opens by identifying soybean (Glycine max) as a member of the Leguminosae (legume/bean) family, botanically also called "Glycine Merr" or by the common name "Soy Bean," and describes it as an ancient crop domesticated in East Asia and later spread worldwide including to the Americas, where it also has industrial (biofuel) uses.

A short world-production history is given: from roughly 10,000 ha of cultivated area in 1804–1804(sic, likely early 1800s) growing steadily, reaching global-scale commercial cultivation by 1765 in the United States per the source's own account (dates as printed in the source, not independently verified), and world soybean product use is described as very diverse — soy milk, soy sauce, tofu, tempeh-style products, and animal feed — the manual gives a per-100g nutrient composition table for soybean (protein, fat, carbohydrate, fiber, ash, and other proximate values) sourced to AVRDC (World Vegetable Center) and ICRISAT reference data.

A health-benefits section lists soybean/soy-product consumption benefits as commonly claimed in extension material: supporting cardiovascular health via lowering LDL cholesterol, being a plant-based alternative for people avoiding animal milk, and general protein nutrition value — presented as farmer/consumer-facing health messaging rather than clinical claims.
